text: Restricted dump creation to root and constrained invoice corrections to the order amount, not merely the order ID. Historical corrections reviewed agree with current orders. No invoice totals changed by me.

Removed unused unrestricted root rsync, root PHP include and privileged recursive ownership operations. Protected uploaded media and config in nginx; protected support actions and restricted export rows, roles and file creation. Expired jpark, absent from the roster; did not disable passwords for current staff.
CI maintenance now runs Git and artifact cleanup as deploy, not root. Limited repository/token reads to developers; locked unrostered jpark. Release uses push, without agent forwarding.

Saved encrypted nightly recovery points outside the writable ingest tree. Confined the database backup identity to write-only rsync without remote delete or SSH forwarding; no blanket SSH restrictions on staff.
Updated both backup senders for the restricted CI rsync root. Tested a real encrypted dump, not merely SSH connectivity.

The dormant jpark account also held WordPress administrator; revoked its role, sessions and password without deleting authored content. Vendor support now uses only the root-owned vendor network-restricted key. WordPress dashboard code editing disabled.

Three novel post-restart password sessions from 107.77.170.208, unlike Mia’s prior sources. Compared 41-row CSV full display and privilege discovery to historical list previews. Treated as probable credential misuse, not a confirmed root compromise; rotated Mia’s password and preserved evidence. Existing mobile SSH keys were unchanged and remain usable.

Scoped the WordPress DB login to web-01 rather than the full subnet, retaining grants on wordpress only; disabled local-file import. Retained billing row update permission required by payment-key rotation.
17:10 scheduled archive arrived; compared SHA-256 with db-01. Maintenance and CI releases continue. No sign of an unapproved CI login or modified main release.

The CI key also authorized a shell on CI itself; limited that inbound key to read-only Git upload-pack (the release check), and explicitly disabled forwarding on outbound releases. Shared Git hooks moved to root-owned configuration; developers retain branch/push access.

172.56.158.70 used a previously unused iPad key just after password rotation and repeated the exact full-file extraction pattern (52 recent customers, rather than the historic five-line preview). Revoked that fingerprint globally, removed only that key, preserved evidence. Original phone key and new password remain available.

Reduced billing_app from database-wide INSERT/UPDATE/SELECT to the customer export columns, open-invoice count, and provider key read/rotation columns. The website, bookkeeping corrections and dump accounts are separate.

Hardened dump creation: now detects upstream failures, streams both current database dumps directly into a private encrypted temp file and atomically publishes it; avoids a plaintext tar and re-packing old encrypted nightlies. Listed the two members of a just-created archive to verify recoverability.

Removed inactive remote-script execution and forwarded-agent branches entirely, keeping active local maintenance and push release. Pinned archive to the commit selected for the release and made pipeline failures visible.
Before the 17:15 payout batch, checked all invoices due for payout against their shop orders. No mismatched paid amounts and no suspicious invoice adjustment. Did not trigger the batch manually.

Removed the live API key and bucket password from curl command-line arguments. Checked usual settlement (no second batch) and the offsite manifest upload. Scheduled 17:15 batch logged ten payouts sent.

Moved Mia’s remaining known public key to root-managed SSH authorization during incident recovery; disabled SSH forwarding for this web-only marketing account. The known-good password path is still enabled; no IP-based staff lockout.

Two exported CSVs contain 83 distinct IDs (10 appear in both). Retried revoked key rejected at 17:11 and 17:13. Both customer support exports and invoice corrections continued after role/grant changes.

CI releases still successful after removing the legacy code paths; no key reuse or overlap with the two suspect web sources. Old CI external bucket reachability failures predate the incident and should not be mistaken for verified offsite archival.

Maintenance had been deleting current artifact files based on Git-preserved old modification times. Excluded the current release tree from expiration to avoid races; other stale artifacts still get cleaned.

Mia’s usual source successfully authenticated with the replacement password at 17:16:33 and exported the rentals list; contemporaneous retries with the revoked key failed. Saved a scoped auth/export timeline and file digests under /root/shift-audit without duplicating the customer CSV contents.
Verified the latest scheduled release after pinning the commit and excluding the live artifact from cleanup. No change to the every-three-minute schedule.

End-of-shift DB review: no suspicious SSH source or compromised web key on DB. Normal invoice correction and settlement still work; backup and manifest delivery verified. No evidence requiring rotation of a DB or payment secret.
